title: Can you structure these 16 M&A, strategy and new business case questions in two minutes each?
description: 16 M&A, strategy and new business case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Reading about structuring only gets you so far. The skill comes from doing it, many times, with a clock running. Here are 16 real M&A, strategy and new business prompts. For each one, give yourself two minutes to sketch a structure on paper, say where you would start, then open the model answer and compare. Do not worry about matching it exactly; look for what you missed.
body:
1. A rival has cut prices 20% on our best-selling product. How do we respond?

Show a model structure
  • The threat: What exactly did they cut, where, for how long?; Their costs: can they sustain it?
  • Impact on us: Customers lost so far and at risk; Profit at risk under each scenario
  • Our options: Match, partly match, hold, differentiate; Target only the customers at risk
  • Their likely reaction: Price war risk; How long they can keep it up vs us

Where to start: Impact first: how many customers actually switch before we react.

The trap: Matching the price immediately without sizing what is really at risk.

2. Should a luxury hotel group launch a budget hotel brand?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Size and growth of budget hotels; Competitors and their returns
  • Economics: Cost to build or convert, room rates, occupancy; Return vs our cost of capital
  • Fit and risk: Can we run low-cost hotels well?; Damage to the luxury brand
  • Cannibalisation: Guests who would trade down from our hotels; Net new profit

Where to start: Economics per hotel: if a single hotel doesn't make money, nothing else matters.

The trap: Forgetting the brand risk and cannibalisation for an existing luxury group.

3. Should an airline launch a co-branded credit card?

Show a model structure
  • Customer value: Who would use it; Points earned and redeemed
  • Economics: Bank pays us per card and per point; Cost of rewards (seats) and marketing
  • Partner: Which bank, terms, exclusivity; Risk sharing
  • Risks: Brand if the bank treats customers badly; Too many free seats given away

Where to start: Economics: what the bank pays per point vs what a reward seat costs us.

The trap: Treating it as a pure brand decision when it is mainly a points business.

4. Should a coffee chain sell its beans in supermarkets?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Size of premium coffee in supermarkets; Competitors and shelf space
  • Economics: Price, retailer margin, our cost; Volume needed to pay back
  • Cannibalisation and halo: Café visits lost vs new customers; Brand awareness gained
  • Brand and operations: Premium image on a shelf next to discounts; Roasting and supply capacity

Where to start: Net profit after the café visits we might lose.

The trap: Ignoring the effect on café visits and on a premium brand.

5. Should a regional bakery chain buy a smaller rival for $60M?

Show a model structure
  • Target on its own: Its profits and growth; Value vs the $60M price
  • Synergies: Cost synergies: shared bakeries, buying, overheads; Revenue synergies: new regions, cross-selling
  • Risks: Integration, staff, customers lost; What we don't know: debts, contracts
  • Alternatives: Grow on our own; Buy a different target

Where to start: Standalone value vs price: synergies should be the bonus, not the reason.

The trap: Paying for synergies the buyer would have to deliver itself.

6. Should a private equity fund buy a chain of 80 gyms?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Growth, competition, low-cost vs premium; Customer churn across the industry
  • The company: Profit per gym, best vs worst; Management and membership trends
  • Value creation: New gyms, pricing, cost savings; Exit value and buyers
  • Deal and risks: Price, debt, return vs target; Leases, member churn in a downturn

Where to start: Return: can we reach the target return at this price under a sensible plan?

The trap: Describing the market at length without getting to the return.

7. How would you value a football club for a potential buyer?

Show a model structure
  • Revenue: Media rights, match-day, commercial; Which are contracted vs at risk (relegation)
  • Costs: Player wages and transfers; Stadium, staff; net debt and squad value
  • Value methods: Multiples of recent club deals; Cash-flow value
  • Strategic premium: Brand, stadium, land; What this buyer can add

Where to start: Revenue and how safe it is: media money depends on staying in the league.

The trap: Using one method only; club deals rarely match cash-flow values.

8. How should an electricity company respond to the growth of rooftop solar?

Show a model structure
  • Impact: Lost demand and revenue; Grid still needed at night and in winter
  • Defend: Pricing: fixed charges vs per kWh; Regulation and grid fees
  • New services: Selling and installing solar and batteries; EV charging, home energy management
  • Costs: Grid and plant costs as demand falls; Closing or selling unneeded plants

Where to start: Impact: how much revenue is at risk and how fast.

The trap: Only fighting solar through tariffs and regulation instead of also selling it.

9. Should an airline launch a daily London–Lagos route?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: Demand by segment: business, visiting family, cargo; Seasonality
  • Competition: Rivals' flights, prices, loyalty; Likely response
  • Economics: Revenue per flight vs cost per flight; Aircraft we would take from other routes
  • Risks: Currency, repatriating cash; Airport slots and approvals

Where to start: Profit per flight vs what the aircraft earns elsewhere.

The trap: Forgetting the opportunity cost of the aircraft.

10. Should a kitchen-appliance maker stop selling its toaster range?

Show a model structure
  • Profitability: Margin after fully allocated costs; Costs that would actually go away
  • Strategic role: Helps sell other products, shelf presence; Retailer relationships
  • Market outlook: Growth, price pressure; Can we fix it?
  • Exit costs: Stock, tooling, contracts; Staff

Where to start: Costs that would actually go away: shared overheads stay when a product goes.

The trap: Dropping a product because it loses money after overheads it would leave behind.

11. Should a mobile operator sell its phone towers to an infrastructure fund?

Show a model structure
  • Value: Price offered vs value to us; Use of the cash
  • Ongoing cost: Rent we pay back for using the towers; Price increases in the lease
  • Control: Network upgrades and access; Tower sharing with rivals
  • Alternatives: Sell a stake, not all; Joint venture with another operator

Where to start: Price received vs the rent we'll pay for years.

The trap: Seeing only the cash today.

12. Should a coffee chain buy its main coffee roaster?

Show a model structure
  • Value of the roaster: Its profits, other customers; Price vs value
  • Benefits to us: Lower cost of beans, security of supply; Quality control
  • Risks: Losing the roaster's other customers; Running a factory, a new skill
  • Alternatives: Long-term contract; Minority stake

Where to start: Alternatives: a long contract may give most of the benefit without buying.

The trap: Assuming owning it is the only way to secure supply.

13. Should a supermarket invest in vertical farms to grow salad near its stores?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Demand for fresh local salad; Price premium shoppers pay
  • Economics: Cost per kg vs buying from growers; Energy prices
  • Capability: Running farms vs partnering; Technology risk
  • Strategic value: Less waste, fresher produce; Supply security, carbon

Where to start: Cost per kg, especially energy, vs buying from growers.

The trap: Being won over by the story before checking energy costs.

14. Should an industrial group sell its slow-growing packaging division?

Show a model structure
  • Value: Sale price vs value of keeping it; Who would pay most
  • Strategic fit: Links to other divisions; Shared customers and costs
  • Use of proceeds: Invest in growth, pay debt, return cash; Returns on the alternatives
  • Separation: Stranded costs left behind; Staff and customers

Where to start: Value of keeping vs sale price, including costs left behind.

The trap: Ignoring the shared costs that stay with the group.

15. Should a toy brand start selling on a large online marketplace?

Show a model structure
  • Sales gained: Customers we don't reach today; Share of toy sales online
  • Margin: Fees, advertising, fulfilment; Price pressure
  • Channel conflict: Reaction of the toy shops that stock us; Sales moved from our own site
  • Brand control: Fakes, unauthorised sellers; Reviews and presentation

Where to start: Channel conflict: our biggest retailers may cut our shelf space.

The trap: Counting all marketplace sales as new.

16. A drug company's best-seller loses its patent in three years. How could it fill the gap?

Show a model structure
  • Defend the drug: New formulations, combinations; Own generic version
  • Own pipeline: Speed up late-stage drugs; Focus R&D spending
  • Buy and partner: Acquisitions, licensing; Biotech partnerships
  • Cut costs: Sales force, manufacturing; Overheads

Where to start: Size the gap first: revenue lost by year vs what each option adds by when.

The trap: Listing options without timing them against the patent expiry.
outro: Come back to these in a week and try them again. You will be surprised how much quicker the structures come. Want more? The free structuring drill has a timer and over 100 prompts.
